payload.title: What Are the Chinese Wedding Traditions You Did Not Know?
payload.excerpt: Chinese wedding traditions in wedding order, from betrothal gifts and the hair-combing ceremony to door games, the tea ceremony and red envelopes, with notes for Australians marrying in China or at home.
key_takeaways: Chinese wedding customs differ by dialect group, region and family, so ask both families which rites they expect before you set the day's order.
In Singapore, most Chinese weddings still begin with guo da li, the betrothal gifts carried from the groom's family to the bride's home on an auspicious day.
In Singapore, the tea ceremony is held at the groom's home and again at the bride's, with tea offered first to the gods and the groom's ancestors, then to his parents and other relatives.

As at November 2026, Smartraveller advises Australians to "Exercise a high degree of caution" in China overall, and a marriage made there can't be registered in Australia, though in most cases it is legally recognised if it was valid there and would have been valid under Australian law.

faq.q: What are the main Chinese wedding traditions?
faq.a: In Singapore's Chinese communities, heritage bodies describe betrothal gifts (guo da li), hair-combing, door games and the tea ceremony, and practice varies by dialect group.

faq.q: What happens at a Chinese wedding tea ceremony?
faq.a: The couple kneel or bow and offer tea to their elders with both hands, in a set order: the gods, the groom's ancestors, his parents, then senior family members and other relatives.
Parents, senior family members and other relatives, at the groom's home and then the bride's.
Shang tou is held the night before in both homes, as a woman of good fortune combs the hair four times with an auspicious phrase each time.

faq.q: What should a guest wear to a Chinese wedding?
faq.a: Red is the primary colour of the ceremonies; families differ on whether guests should wear it, so ask the couple.

faq.q: Do guests give red envelopes at a Chinese wedding?
faq.a: Red envelopes (hong bao, lai see) are made for gifts of money at weddings; guest custom varies by family.

faq.q: Can Australians get married in China?
faq.a: Check first: as at November 2026, ask the embassy whether you need a CNI, and ask the registry and the embassy which documents, translations and fees apply.
